title: How crumple zones make crashes gentler
examples: Why are cars designed to crumple?
Why doesn't a car's cabin crush?

explain.say: In a crash the car and everyone in it must lose all their speed. That change is fixed, but the force depends on how quickly it happens: stop twice as slowly and the force is halved.

explain.say: So the front and back of a car are designed to fold up in a controlled way, like a concertina. Crushing takes a fraction of a second longer, so the force on the passengers drops, and the bending metal soaks up energy.

faq.q: Why would a rigid car be more dangerous?
faq.a: A rigid car stops almost instantly when it hits something, so everyone inside must lose their speed in a tiny time. That needs an enormous force on their bodies.
asks: Would a stronger car be safer?

faq.a: A crumple zone is the front or back part of a car designed to crush in a controlled way in a crash. It makes the car take longer to stop and soaks up energy as the metal bends.
asks: Why are cars designed to crumple?

faq.q: How do seatbelts and airbags add to a crumple zone?
faq.a: They make your own body slow down more gradually. The belt stretches a little and the airbag squashes as you press in, adding time and spreading the force over a bigger area.
asks: Do seatbelts work with crumple zones?

faq.q: Why does a longer stopping time mean a smaller force?
faq.a: Force equals the change in momentum divided by the time it takes. The change is set by the car's mass and speed, so spreading it over twice the time halves the force.
asks: What is the physics of crumple zones?

faq.q: Why doesn't the whole car crumple?
faq.a: The middle of the car, the safety cell, is made of very strong steel so it keeps a space around the people inside. Only the front and back are meant to crush.
asks: Why doesn't a car's cabin crush?

facts: Crumple zones were invented by Mercedes-Benz engineer Béla Barényi and first used in a production car in 1959.
Force equals change in momentum divided by the time taken.
A car badly crumpled after a crash has often done its job of protecting the people inside.
